abnormal: Unusual changes in the eye's appearance or function, such as odd shapes, unexpected colors, or unusual blood vessels.
amd: Age-related macular degeneration with yellowish spots, color changes, and abnormal blood vessels in the central retina.
arteriosclerotic retinopathy: Narrowing of retinal blood vessels with a shiny appearance and changes where arteries and veins meet.
blood vessel abnormalities: Irregular blood vessel shapes or unusual patterns, like twists, loops, or abnormal branching.
central serous retinopathy: Fluid buildup under the retina, causing a raised dome-like area in the central retina.
choroidal neovascularization: New abnormal blood vessels in the central retina, causing bleeding and fluid buildup in the macula.
diabetes: Can lead to diabetic retinopathy, showing tiny red dots, small bleeds, and new abnormal blood vessels in the retina.
diabetic retinopathy: Changes in the retinal blood vessels, with tiny red dots, small bleeds, white fluffy spots, and new blood vessels.
drusen: Small yellowish deposits under the retina.
glaucoma: Increased optic disc cupping with a larger cup-to-disc ratio, indicating optic nerve damage.
hard exudates: Bright yellowish-white deposits in the retina, often forming rings or clusters.
hemorrhage: Bleeding in the retina, ranging from small red dots to larger dark red areas.
hypertension: Changes in retinal blood vessels due to high blood pressure, with narrowed blood vessels and changes at crossing points of arteries and veins.
hypertensive retinopathy: Blood vessel changes in the retina due to high blood pressure, with narrowed blood vessels, crossing changes, and reflective blood vessels.
laser scar: Whitish retinal mark from laser treatment, used to treat tears or leaks.
macular edema: Swelling in the central part of the retina (macula) due to fluid leakage from blood vessels, causing blurred or distorted vision.
media opacity: Cloudiness or obstruction in the media (lens, cornea, or vitreous), leading to blurry or unclear retinal view.
microaneurysms: Tiny bulges in the blood vessels of the retina, appearing as small round red dots.
mild diabetic retinopathy: Early changes in the blood vessels of the retina, with scattered tiny red dots and small bleeds.
moderate diabetic retinopathy: More extensive damage to the blood vessels of the retina, with larger bleeds, more numerous red dots, and retinal swelling.
myopic macular degeneration: Thinning of the retina and choroid with visible pigment changes, especially in high myopia.
nevus: A benign, pigmented spot on the retina, similar to a mole on the skin.
optic disc cupping: Deepened optic cup and larger cup-to-disc ratio, indicating possible glaucoma.
optic disc edema: Swelling of the optic disc with blurred edges and redness.
optic disc pallor: Pale optic disc, indicating damage to the optic nerve.
papilledema: Swelling of the optic disc due to increased intracranial pressure, often associated with headaches and vision changes.
proliferative diabetic retinopathy: Extensive new blood vessels and bleeding in the retina or vitreous.
pseudopapilledema: The optic disc may appear elevated or swollen, but the edges are well-defined.
retinal artery occlusion: Pale retinal area with possible cherry-red spot; may show hemorrhages.
retinal detachment: Elevated, grayish retina with possible folds, tears, or fluid.
retinitis: Inflamed retina with swelling and color changes.
severe diabetic retinopathy: Advanced diabetic eye disease with numerous new blood vessels and areas of retinal detachment.
soft exudates: Soft fluffy spots in the retina, appearing as white or grayish fluffy spots.
tessellation: Visible choroidal blood vessels near the central retina.
normal: Healthy retina with clear and well-defined structures and no abnormalities.
